title: Love and argument
hook: Jews hold many views on Israel's politics; some love it, some criticize it, some do both

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sadat's flight into war and peace, and your line: seek peace. Did you take one step toward peace in a quarrel? Today, the argument that doesn't stop, and the love underneath it. Day one thousand thirty-five.

A Shabbat dinner table. The candles are lit, the bread is blessed, and somewhere around the soup someone mentions Israel's government. One cousin is furious at it. An uncle defends it, louder. A grandmother says she loves the country and is worried sick about it. Somebody's new partner, at the table for the first time, wonders whether to say anything at all. Nobody leaves. The arguing goes on through the chicken. Dessert still comes. Today: love and argument.
screen: `A SHABBAT TABLE.` → `A COUSIN, AN UNCLE, A GRANDMOTHER.` → `NOBODY LEAVES.`

segments.voice: Ask Jews about Israel's politics and you will hear many views. Some love the country and defend its choices. Some love it and criticize it hard. Some feel far from it. Some do several of these at once. Arguing hard is not new in this tradition. The Talmud is built out of disagreements, with the losing side's view kept on the page. The house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, two schools of rabbis, argued for years. The Talmud says a heavenly voice finally declared that both were the words of the living God, but the law would follow Hillel. Why Hillel? Because, the Talmud says, they were kind and humble, and they taught Shammai's view too, even putting it before their own. The Mishnah draws a line through all arguing. An argument for the sake of heaven will last; one that isn't, won't. Its example of a good argument: Hillel and Shammai. Its example of a bad one: Korah and his followers, who argued with Moses to grab power. And the Torah puts love and honest challenge in a single verse. It begins, "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart," and in the same breath tells you to speak up when your neighbor does wrong. Read that way, criticism and love are not opposites, and keeping quiet can be a way of giving up on someone. The question is the one the Mishnah asks: is this for the sake of heaven, to understand, or just to win? This lesson won't tell you what to think about Israel. It describes a very old way of arguing: loudly, honestly, at the same table, staying for dessert.
screen: `MANY VIEWS AT ONE TABLE.` · `THESE AND THESE ARE WORDS OF GOD.` · `FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN.` · `LOVE AND REBUKE IN ONE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: listen to a view unlike yours. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who sees something important very differently from you: politics, faith, family. Picture them across a table. In your mind, let them speak first, and try to say their view back in a way they'd call fair, the way the house of Hillel taught the other side's words. You don't have to agree. Just listen until you understand. The bell holds the time.
Hillel, whose school argued for years with Shammai's, and whose kindness and humility won the law's final word. Today's word.
Your line: love and argue. Today, in one disagreement, say the other person's view back to them fairly before you give your own. Day one thousand thirty-five.

howItsDone: Jews study Talmud in pairs, called chavruta, arguing over the text together, and the Mishnah's ideal of an argument 'for the sake of heaven' is often cited for disagreements in the community.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'many love it, many criticize it, many do both' was changed to 'some' in the hook field and the voice; 'you will hear many views' describes views, not a share of Jews.

Eruvin 13b is paraphrased (the heavenly voice, 'these and these are the words of the living God', the law following Hillel because they were kind and humble and taught Shammai's words first); the number of years they argued is omitted. Please check.
Pirkei Avot 5:17 is paraphrased (numbering differs between editions; some number it 5:20).
The second half of Leviticus 19:17 is paraphrased; only the first clause is quoted from JPS 1917.
The lesson takes no side on Israel's politics; please check it reads that way to readers across the spectrum.
howItsDone mentions chavruta study; please confirm.
Editor pass: fixed a garbled hook line ('duck under it'); replaced 'None of this is new' (which seemed to date views on a modern state) with a claim about arguing in the tradition.

Audit pass: 'In this tradition, criticism and love are not opposites. Silence can be a way of giving up on someone' was the narrator's own verdict; it is now tied to the verse ('Read that way...'). Eruvin 13b and Avot 5:17 checked: the paraphrases match. 'Argued with Moses to grab power' is an interpretation of Korah, not the Mishnah's words; a Keeper may soften.
